intro: How long is your desk? What time is lunch? How much is in your pocket? Every day you measure things. This unit shows you how. You will lay units end to end. You will read a ruler in inches and centimeters. You will make a graph of what you find.

Then you will learn the clock. The short hand tells the hour. The long hand counts minutes by fives. You will know when it is 3:00 and when it is 3:30. You will know the difference between a.m. and p.m.
Last, you will count coins. Pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters each have a value. You will add them up, buy things and give change. By the end, you can run a bake sale table all by yourself.
bigQuestion: How do we use numbers to say how long, what time and how much?

timeline.t: Wake up. The short hand is on the 7, the long hand on the 12.
School starts. The long hand points to the 6: half past 8.
Measure the hallway in shoes, then in feet with a tape.
Make a bar graph of everyone's shoe lengths.
Lunch. The clock hands both point straight up.
Sort the bake sale coins: quarters, dimes, nickels, pennies.
Count the coins. Big coins first: 25, 35, 45, 50.
A cookie costs 35¢. Count up to make change from 50¢.
The bell rings. School is over for the day.
Dinner. Tell someone at home what time it is.

words.d: the one thing you use over and over to measure, like a cube or an inch
a small unit of length; a paper clip is about 1 inch
a unit of length equal to 12 inches
a small unit of length, about the width of a pinky finger; 100 make a meter
a graph with bars; a taller bar means a bigger count
the short hand on a clock; it points to the hour
the smallest amount of U.S. money; a penny is one cent
the money you get back when you pay more than the price

test.q: Two sticks start at the same line. The blue stick sticks out past the other one. Which is longer?
test.why: With the ends lined up, the stick that reaches farther is longer. That is the blue one.

test.q: You measure a table with cubes. The cubes overlap. What happens to your count?
test.why: Overlapping cubes each cover less new space. More cubes fit, so the count is too big.

test.q: How many inches are in one foot?
test.why: One foot is 12 inches. A 12-inch ruler is one foot long.

test.q: How many centimeters are in one meter?
A picture graph shows 5 apples and 3 bananas. How many more apples than bananas?
test.why: 5 − 3 = 2 more apples. Adding gives 8, which is the total.

test.q: The short hand is between 2 and 3. The long hand is on the 6. What time is it?
test.why: Long hand on 6 means half past. The short hand passed the 2, so it is 2:30.

test.q: The long hand points to the 10. How many minutes past the hour is it?
test.why: Count by fives to the 10: 10 fives is 50. It is 50 minutes past.

test.q: One quarter and two dimes. How many cents?
A pencil costs 30¢. A pen costs 45¢. How much for both?
A snack costs 65¢. You pay with three quarters, 75¢. How much change do you get?
test.why: Count up from 65 to 75. That is 10. Check: 75 − 65 = 10.

write.prompt: You have one quarter, two dimes and one nickel. You buy a cookie for 35¢. How much money do you have? How much is left after you buy the cookie? Explain each step.
tips: Count the coins big to small: 25, 35, 45, 50.
Check by counting up from 35 to 50.
Say why your answer makes sense.

title: Measuring, Time and Money

chapters.title: Length and Data
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we measure how long something is and show what we found?

story.title: The Hallway in Shoes
story.kicker: A class measures the same hallway two ways and gets two very different numbers.
paragraphs: Ms. Ruiz's class had a question. How long is the hallway outside the room? Nobody knew. Amir had an idea. He took off one shoe. He set it on the floor by the wall. Then he set his other shoe in front of it, heel to toe.

Amir walked the hallway shoe by shoe. His friends counted with him. At the far wall he stopped. The count was 40 shoes. Then Nia tried it with her shoes. Her shoes were smaller. Her count was 50 shoes. The class was puzzled.

Ms. Ruiz brought out a long tape measure. It had numbers on it. Two students held the ends. They read the number at the far wall. The hallway was 30 feet long. Every student got 30 feet, no matter who held the tape.
Amir looked at the two numbers. Forty shoes. Fifty shoes. Thirty feet. The hallway had not changed at all. Only the unit had changed. That afternoon the class made a graph of everyone's shoe lengths.
story.think: Why did Amir and Nia get different numbers for the same hallway?

lessons.title: Longer and Shorter
lessons.mainIdea: To compare two lengths, line up one end, then look at the other end.
reading: Maya has a red crayon and a blue crayon. Which one is *longer*? She puts them side by side. She lines up the left ends. Now she looks at the right ends. The red crayon sticks out more. So the red crayon is longer. The blue crayon is *shorter*.
Lining up the ends matters. If one crayon starts ahead, you get fooled. A short crayon can look long. Always start both objects at the same line. Then compare the other ends.
Try it with a pencil and a marker. Line up the ends. Which one sticks out? That one is longer. If neither one sticks out, they are the same length.

words.d: reaching farther than the other object when the ends are lined up
not reaching as far as the other object when the ends are lined up

look.title: Two Pencils on a Desk
look.text: Picture two pencils on a desk. Their left ends touch the same line. The yellow pencil ends at the 4 on a ruler. The green pencil ends at the 6. Neither pencil has been moved.
look.prompt: Which pencil is longer? How do you know?

check.q: Two ribbons start at the same line. The blue ribbon sticks out past the red one. Which ribbon is longer?
check.why: The ends are lined up, so the ribbon that sticks out farther is longer. That is the blue one.

check.q: Why do you line up the ends before you compare?
check.why: If one object starts ahead, it looks longer than it is. Lining up the ends makes it fair.

check.q: A pencil is longer than a crayon. The crayon is longer than an eraser. Which is shortest?
check.why: Pencil is longer than crayon, and crayon is longer than eraser. So the eraser is the shortest of the three.

lessons.title: Putting Three in Order
lessons.mainIdea: Order lengths from shortest to longest by comparing two at a time.
reading: Leo has three sticks. The brown stick is 5 cubes long. The gray stick is 8 cubes long. The white stick is 3 cubes long. He wants to line them up from shortest to longest.
Compare two at a time. 3 is less than 5, so white goes before brown. 5 is less than 8, so brown goes before gray. The *order* is white, brown, gray. Shortest to longest: 3, 5, 8.
You can also order without numbers. Line up the ends. Find the shortest one. Set it first. Then find the next shortest. Keep going until all of them are in a row.

words.d: a line-up that goes from shortest to longest, or longest to shortest

look.title: Leo's Three Sticks
look.cite: Leo's sticks, measured in one-inch cubes (example)
look.prompt: Which stick is in the middle when you put them in order?

check.q: Three ropes are 4 feet, 9 feet and 6 feet long. Which order is shortest to longest?
check.why: 4 is less than 6, and 6 is less than 9. So the order is 4, 6, 9.

check.q: A jump rope is 7 feet. A scarf is 3 feet. A ladder is 10 feet. Which is longest?
check.why: 10 is more than 7 and more than 3. The ladder, at 10 feet, is longest.

check.q: Sam's pencil is longer than Ana's. Ana's pencil is longer than Kim's. Whose pencil is in the middle?
check.why: Sam's is longest and Kim's is shortest. Ana's is between them, so it is in the middle.

lessons.title: Units End to End
lessons.mainIdea: Measure by laying same-size units end to end with no gaps and no overlaps.
reading: How long is the book? Rosa uses paper clips. She lays them in a line along the edge. Each clip touches the next. No *gap*. No overlap. She counts 6 clips. The book is 6 paper clips long.
The clips must all be the same size. Big and small clips mixed give a wrong count. Gaps make the count too small. Overlaps make it too big. Start at one end. Stop at the other end.
A different *unit* gives a different number. The same book is 6 big clips long. It is 9 small clips long. The book did not change. The unit changed. A smaller unit means more units.

words.d: the one thing you use over and over to measure, like a paper clip or a cube
an empty space between two units that should be touching

look.title: Two Ways to Lay Cubes
look.text: Look at a crayon box. Ben lays 4 cubes along it, end to end, with no gaps. Jo lays 4 cubes too, but she leaves spaces between them. Her cubes reach past the end of the box.

check.q: Tia measures a shelf with cubes. She leaves gaps between the cubes. What happens to her count?
check.why: Gaps take up space that no cube covers. Fewer cubes fit, so the count is too small.

check.q: A desk is 5 long shoes long. You measure it again with short shoes. What happens?
check.why: Short shoes cover less space each. It takes more of them to reach the end of the desk.

check.q: Which rule is a good rule for measuring?
check.why: Same-size units that touch end to end give a true count. Gaps and mixed sizes give wrong counts.

lessons.title: Inches and Feet
lessons.mainIdea: An inch is a small unit. A foot is 12 inches. Use a ruler to measure.
reading: A *ruler* has marks. Each mark is one *inch*. Put the 0 end at one end of the object. Read the number at the other end. A marker ends at the 7. The marker is 7 inches long.
A *foot* is 12 inches. Your math book is about 1 foot long. A door is about 7 feet tall. Use inches for small things. Use feet for big things, like a rug or a room.
Do not start at the 1 mark. Start at 0. If you start at 1, your number is one too big. A crayon that ends at 5 looks like 5 inches. But it is only 4 inches.

words.d: a small unit of length; a paper clip is about 1 inch long
a unit of length equal to 12 inches; a math book is about 1 foot
a flat stick with marks for measuring inches or centimeters

look.title: Feet and Inches
look.prompt: How many inches are in 2 feet? How do you know?

check.q: A pencil starts at 0 on a ruler and ends at the 6. How long is it?
check.why: Starting at 0 and ending at 6 means 6 inches. From 0 to 6 is 6 inch marks.

check.q: How many inches are in 1 foot?
check.why: One foot is 12 inches. A 12-inch ruler is exactly one foot long.

check.q: Which is best measured in feet?
check.why: A rug is big. Feet are the bigger unit, so feet fit a rug. Clips and crayons use inches.

lessons.title: Centimeters and Meters
lessons.mainIdea: A centimeter is smaller than an inch. A meter is 100 centimeters.
reading: A *centimeter* is a small unit. It is about the width of your pinky finger. Many rulers show centimeters on one side. A paper clip is about 3 centimeters long.
A *meter* is 100 centimeters. A baseball bat is about 1 meter long. A door is about 2 meters tall. Use a meter stick for big things. Use a centimeter ruler for small things.
Measure a pencil twice. In inches it is 6. In centimeters it is 15. Centimeters are smaller, so you need more of them. Both numbers are right. They just use different units.

words.d: a small unit of length, about the width of a pinky finger
a unit of length equal to 100 centimeters, about one big step

look.title: One Book, Two Numbers
look.text: Nadia measures a book twice. With the inch side of the ruler, it is 10 inches. With the centimeter side, it is 25 centimeters. The book did not grow between the two measurements.
look.prompt: Why is the centimeter number bigger than the inch number?

check.q: How many centimeters are in 1 meter?
check.why: One meter is 100 centimeters. A meter stick has 100 centimeter marks.

check.q: A ribbon is 4 inches long. You measure it again in centimeters. What happens to the number?
check.why: A centimeter is smaller than an inch. It takes more centimeters to cover the ribbon, so the number is bigger.

check.q: Which tool is best for measuring a hallway?
check.why: A hallway is long. A meter stick is the biggest tool here, so it takes the fewest moves.

lessons.title: Estimate, Then Measure
lessons.mainIdea: An estimate is a careful guess. Use something you know as a guide.
reading: An *estimate* is a careful guess. You know a paper clip is about 1 inch. A crayon looks about 4 clips long. So your estimate is about 4 inches. Then you measure. It is 4 inches. Good estimate!
Big things need a bigger guide. Your math book is about 1 foot. A desk looks like 2 books. Estimate: about 2 feet. Then measure it. If it is 2 feet, your guess was close.
Estimates do not have to be exact. Close is good. If you guess 20 feet and it is 3 feet, think again. Pick a better guide. Then guess again.

words.d: a careful guess about a size or amount, made before you measure

look.title: Good Guides for Guessing
look.cite: Everyday classroom objects, rounded to the nearest inch
look.prompt: A desk looks like 3 rulers long. About how many inches is that?

check.q: A paper clip is about 1 inch. A marker looks like 5 clips long. About how long is the marker?
check.why: 5 clips at about 1 inch each is about 5 inches. Feet would be far too big for a marker.

check.q: What is an estimate?
check.why: An estimate is a careful guess you make before measuring. It does not have to be exact.

check.q: A rug looks like 6 math books long. A math book is about 1 foot. About how long is the rug?
check.why: 6 books at about 1 foot each is about 6 feet.

lessons.title: Picture Graphs and Bar Graphs
lessons.mainIdea: A graph shows counts with pictures or bars so you can compare fast.
reading: The class votes on a favorite pet. Dog gets 6 votes. Cat gets 4. Fish gets 2. A *picture graph* shows one picture for each vote. The dog row has 6 pictures. The cat row has 4.
A *bar graph* uses bars instead of pictures. A taller bar means more. The dog bar goes up to 6. The fish bar goes up to 2. You can see the winner fast. Dog wins.
Graphs answer questions. How many more dogs than cats? 6 − 4 = 2. How many votes in all? 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. Read the numbers off the graph. Then add or subtract.

words.d: a graph that uses one small picture for each thing counted
a graph that uses bars; a taller or longer bar means a bigger count

look.title: Favorite Pet Votes
look.prompt: How many more votes did dog get than fish?

check.q: A graph shows dog 6, cat 4, fish 2. How many more dogs than cats?
check.why: 6 − 4 = 2. Adding gives 10, which is a different question.

check.q: Dog 6, cat 4, fish 2. How many votes in all?
check.why: 6 + 4 = 10, then 10 + 2 = 12 votes in all.

check.q: In a bar graph, which bar shows the biggest count?
check.why: Bars grow with the count. The tallest bar stands for the biggest number.

lessons.title: Line Plots
lessons.mainIdea: A line plot puts an X above each measurement on a number line.
reading: The class measures pencils in inches. The lengths are 5, 6, 6, 7, 6, 5. A *line plot* shows them. Draw a number line from 5 to 7. Put an X above the number for each pencil.
Above 5 there are 2 X's. Above 6 there are 3 X's. Above 7 there is 1 X. The tallest stack shows the most common length. That is 6 inches.
Count all the X's to find how many pencils. 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 pencils. How many pencils are longer than 5 inches? Count the X's above 6 and 7. 3 + 1 = 4.

words.d: a number line with an X above a number for each measurement

look.title: Pencil Lengths
look.prompt: How many pencils are shorter than 7 inches?

check.q: A line plot has 2 X's above 5, 3 above 6 and 1 above 7. Which length is most common?
check.why: The tallest stack is above 6, with 3 X's. So 6 inches is most common.

check.q: Same plot: 2 X's above 5, 3 above 6, 1 above 7. How many pencils in all?
check.why: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 pencils.

check.q: Same plot. How many pencils are longer than 5 inches?
check.why: Longer than 5 means the X's above 6 and 7. 3 + 1 = 4.

review.q: Two straws start at the same line. The green straw sticks out past the pink one. Which straw is shorter?
review.why: The green straw reaches farther, so it is longer. The pink straw is shorter.

review.q: Ivan measures a table with cubes. He leaves gaps between them. What is his count?
review.why: Gaps leave space with no cube in it. Fewer cubes fit, so the count is too small.

review.q: How many inches are in 1 foot?
review.why: One foot is 12 inches. 100 is centimeters in a meter.

review.q: A pencil is 6 inches long. You measure it in centimeters. The new number is...
review.why: Centimeters are smaller than inches, so more of them fit. The number is bigger, about 15.

review.q: A bar graph shows red 5, blue 3, green 4. How many votes in all?
A line plot has 1 X above 4, 4 X's above 5 and 2 X's above 6. Which length is most common?
review.why: The tallest stack is above 5, with 4 X's.

chapters.title: Time and Money
chapters.bigQuestion: How do clocks and coins help us know what time it is and how much we have?

story.title: The Clock and the Cash Box
story.kicker: One clock on the wall and one box of coins run the whole day in Room 12.
paragraphs: Every morning in Room 12, Dev looks at the clock over the door. The short hand points at the 9. The long hand points at the 12. It is 9:00. That means lunch count time. Dev counts hands. Twelve kids want hot lunch. He writes 12 on the slip.

The clock keeps going. At 9:30 the long hand points down at the 6. Reading time. At 10:15 the long hand is on the 3. Math time. Dev likes to say the times out loud. His teacher says the clock is a map of the day.

On Friday the class holds a bake sale. Cookies cost 25 cents. Juice costs 50 cents. Dev sits by the cash box. A girl hands him three dimes for a cookie. He counts: 10, 20, 30. That is more than 25. He counts up from 25 to 30. He gives her back a nickel.

At 3:00 p.m. the bell rings. Dev counts the cash box. Quarters first, then dimes, then nickels, then pennies. The class made $6.75. The clock said the day was over. The coins said the sale was a success.
story.think: Why did Dev count the quarters before the pennies?

lessons.title: Hour and Half Hour
lessons.mainIdea: The short hand tells the hour. Long hand on 12 means o'clock; long hand on 6 means half past.
reading: A clock has two hands. The short hand is the *hour hand*. The long hand is the *minute hand*. When the long hand points to 12, it is o'clock. Short hand on 3, long hand on 12: 3 o'clock. We write 3:00.
When the long hand points to 6, it is *half past*. The short hand sits between two numbers. It is between 3 and 4, so it is half past 3. We write 3:30. Thirty minutes is half an hour.
A digital clock shows only numbers. 3:00 means 3 o'clock. 3:30 means half past 3. Watch out: at 3:30 the short hand is past the 3, not on it. Use the number it just passed.

words.d: the short hand on a clock; it points to the hour
the long hand on a clock; it shows the minutes
30 minutes after the hour; the long hand points to the 6

look.title: The Clock on the Wall
look.text: Look at the clock on the wall. The short hand is between the 7 and the 8. The long hand points straight down at the 6. The class is just finishing breakfast.
look.prompt: What time is it? How do you write it with numbers?

check.q: The short hand is on 5. The long hand is on 12. What time is it?
check.why: Long hand on 12 means o'clock. Short hand on 5 means 5. So it is 5:00.

check.q: The short hand is between 8 and 9. The long hand is on 6. What time is it?
check.why: Long hand on 6 means half past. The short hand passed the 8, so it is 8:30.

check.q: How many minutes are in half an hour?
check.why: An hour is 60 minutes. Half of 60 is 30.

lessons.title: Five Minutes at a Time
lessons.mainIdea: Each number on the clock is 5 minutes. Count by fives from the 12.
reading: The long hand moves around the clock. Each number it passes is 5 *minutes*. Count by fives from the 12. At the 1 it is 5 minutes. At the 2 it is 10. At the 3 it is 15. At the 6 it is 30.
Short hand just past 2, long hand on the 4. Count: 5, 10, 15, 20. It is 2:20. Short hand near 10, long hand on the 9. Count: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45. It is 9:45.
Read the short hand first. Use the number it passed. Then count the long hand by fives. A common mistake is reading the long hand as 4 instead of 20. The number is a helper, not the minutes.

words.d: a short bit of time; 60 minutes make one hour

look.title: Where the Long Hand Points
look.cite: Counting by fives around a clock face
look.prompt: The long hand is on the 7. How many minutes is that?

check.q: The long hand points to the 8. How many minutes past the hour is it?
check.why: Count by fives to the 8: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40. It is 40 minutes.

check.q: The short hand is just past 4. The long hand is on the 2. What time is it?
check.why: The hour is 4. Long hand on the 2 is 5, 10. So it is 4:10.

check.q: The short hand is near 6. The long hand is on the 11. What time is it?
check.why: The hour is 6. Count by fives to the 11: 11 fives is 55. So it is 6:55.

lessons.title: Morning, Noon and Night
lessons.mainIdea: A.M. is morning, before noon. P.M. is afternoon and evening, after noon.
reading: A day has 24 hours. The clock goes around twice. *A.M.* means the hours from midnight to noon. *P.M.* means the hours from noon to midnight. 7:00 a.m. is breakfast time. 7:00 p.m. is close to bedtime.
Look at a school day. School starts at 8:30 a.m. Lunch is at 12:00. That is *noon*. Recess is at 1:15 p.m. School ends at 3:00 p.m. Dinner is at 6:00 p.m.
A schedule is a list of times. It tells what comes next. Reading is at 9:00 a.m. Math is at 10:00 a.m. Math comes after reading. The earlier time always comes first.

words.d: the hours from midnight to noon; the morning
the hours from noon to midnight; afternoon, evening and night
12:00 in the middle of the day, when a.m. changes to p.m.

look.title: One School Day
look.cite: Example schedule for one school day

check.q: You eat breakfast at 7:00. Is it a.m. or p.m.?
check.why: Breakfast is in the morning, before noon. Morning hours are a.m.

check.q: What do we call 12:00 in the middle of the day?
check.why: Noon is 12:00 in the daytime. Midnight is 12:00 at night.

check.q: Music is at 1:00 p.m. Art is at 10:00 a.m. Which comes first?
choices: they are at the same time
check.why: 10:00 a.m. is in the morning. 1:00 p.m. is after noon. Art comes first.

lessons.title: What Each Coin Is Worth
lessons.mainIdea: A penny is 1 cent, a nickel 5 cents, a dime 10 cents, a quarter 25 cents.
reading: A penny is worth 1 *cent*. A nickel is worth 5 cents. A dime is worth 10 cents. A quarter is worth 25 cents. We write cents with a ¢ sign. 5¢ means 5 cents.
Size can fool you. A dime is the smallest *coin*. But it is worth more than a penny or a nickel. A nickel is bigger than a dime but worth less. Look at the coin, not its size.
Two nickels make 10 cents, the same as one dime. 5 + 5 = 10. Five pennies make one nickel. Two dimes and a nickel make 25 cents. 10 + 10 + 5 = 25. That is the same as one quarter.

words.d: the smallest amount of U.S. money; a penny is one cent
a small round piece of metal money, like a penny or a dime

look.title: U.S. Coins
look.prompt: How many nickels make one quarter?

check.q: Which coin is worth 10 cents?
check.why: A dime is 10 cents. A nickel is 5 and a quarter is 25.

check.q: How many pennies equal one nickel?
check.why: A nickel is 5 cents. Five pennies at 1 cent each make 5 cents.

check.q: Which is worth more, a dime or a nickel?
choices: the nickel, because it is bigger
the dime, because it is 10 cents
check.why: A dime is 10 cents and a nickel is 5 cents. The dime is small but worth more.

lessons.title: Counting Mixed Coins
lessons.mainIdea: Start with the biggest coins. Count on by 25, 10, 5, then 1.
reading: Jamal has a quarter, a dime and two pennies. Start with the biggest coin. Quarter: 25. *Count on* with the dime: 35. Add a penny: 36. Add a penny: 37. He has 37 cents.
Sort first. Put quarters, then dimes, then nickels, then pennies. Two dimes and three nickels: 10, 20, then 25, 30, 35. That is 35 cents. Big coins first keeps the numbers easy.
Check by counting a different way. Three nickels are 15. Two dimes are 20. 15 + 20 = 35. Same answer. If your two counts do not match, count again.

words.d: start at one number and keep counting up from there

look.title: Coins in a Hand
look.text: Picture a hand holding coins: one quarter, two dimes, one nickel and one penny. Say the count out loud, big coins first: 25, 35, 45, 50, 51.
look.prompt: How much money is in the hand? Now count it a second way to check.

check.q: One quarter and one dime. How many cents?
Two dimes and one nickel. How many cents?
One quarter, one nickel and two pennies. How many cents?

lessons.title: Money Word Problems
lessons.mainIdea: 100 cents make 1 dollar. Add or subtract cents to solve money problems.
reading: A *dollar* is 100 cents. Four quarters make a dollar: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100. We write one dollar as $1.00. We write 45 cents as 45¢ or as $0.45.
Mia buys a pencil for 30¢ and an eraser for 15¢. How much in all? 30 + 15 = 45. She pays 45¢. Kai has 50¢ and spends 20¢. How much is left? 50 − 20 = 30. He has 30¢ left.
Read the question twice. In all means add. Left means subtract. Draw the coins if it helps. Then check your work: 30 + 15 = 45, and 45 − 15 = 30. It matches.

words.d: 100 cents; four quarters or ten dimes make one dollar

look.title: At the Bake Sale Table
look.text: The bake sale sells cookies for 25¢ and juice for 50¢. Priya buys one cookie and one juice. She hands over three quarters and waits.
look.prompt: How much does Priya spend? Did she pay the right amount?

check.q: A sticker costs 40¢. A pencil costs 35¢. How much for both?
check.why: 40 + 35 = 75. Both together cost 75¢.

check.q: Lily has 80¢. She spends 30¢. How much is left?
check.why: 80 − 30 = 50. She has 50¢ left.

check.q: How many quarters make one dollar?
check.why: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100 cents, which is one dollar. That is 4 quarters.

lessons.title: Making Change by Counting Up
lessons.mainIdea: To make change, count up from the price to the money paid.
reading: A cookie costs 35¢. Tom pays with two quarters, 50¢. How much *change* does he get? Count up from 35. From 35 to 40 is a nickel. From 40 to 50 is a dime. 5 + 10 = 15. Tom gets 15¢ back.
Check with subtraction. 50 − 35 = 15. Same answer. Counting up is like climbing stairs. Start at the price. Stop at the money paid. The steps you took are the change.
Try another one. Juice is 60¢. Ana pays $1.00. Count up: 60 to 70 is 10. 70 to 100 is 30. 10 + 30 = 40. The change is 40¢. Check: 100 − 60 = 40. Yes.

words.d: the money you get back when you pay more than the price

look.title: A Muffin and Two Quarters
look.text: A muffin costs 45¢. Sam pays with two quarters, which is 50¢. The seller counts up out loud: 45, and one nickel makes 50.
look.prompt: How much change does Sam get? Check it with subtraction.

check.q: A pencil costs 20¢. You pay with a quarter. How much change do you get?
check.why: Count up from 20 to 25. That is 5. Check: 25 − 20 = 5.

check.q: Gum costs 70¢. You pay with $1.00. How much change do you get?
check.why: Count up from 70 to 100. That is 30. Check: 100 − 70 = 30.

check.q: Why do we count up from the price?
choices: to find how many coins we have
check.why: Counting up from the price to the money paid shows how much comes back. That is the change.

review.q: The short hand is on 9. The long hand is on 12. What time is it?
review.why: Long hand on 12 means o'clock. Short hand on 9 means 9:00.

review.q: The long hand points to the 3. How many minutes past the hour is it?
review.why: Count by fives: 5, 10, 15. The 3 means 15 minutes.

review.q: Bedtime is 8:00 at night. Is that a.m. or p.m.?
review.why: Night hours come after noon, so 8:00 at night is p.m.

review.q: One dime and three pennies. How many cents?
A toy costs 60¢. A ball costs 25¢. How much for both?
Bread costs 40¢. You pay 50¢. What is your change?
review.why: Count up from 40 to 50. That is 10. Check: 50 − 40 = 10.
